summary: This Experimental document defines a BFD Optimized Authentication Mode called Meticulous Keyed ISAAC. It authenticates some BFD packets with less CPU time than MD5 or SHA-1, at a cost in security. It cannot signal state changes but can keep a session in the Up state.

plainLanguage.summary: BFD checks that a link is alive by sending packets very often. Signing every one of them with a cryptographic hash costs more CPU than some small routers can spare. This RFC gives a cheaper proof that the packets really came from the other end: both ends run the same random number generator, and each packet carries the number that generator would produce for it.

questions: why does bfd use isaac for authentication
subtitle: A cheap way to prove a BFD session is still up, without hashing every packet.

tldr.problem: BFD can authenticate its packets with MD5 or SHA-1, but those hashes are expensive on constrained hardware, and on a fast BFD session the CPU cost is significant.
tldr.mechanism: The receiver and sender run the same pseudorandom number generator, seeded from a shared key, and each packet carries the 32-bit number that generator produces for that packet's sequence number.
tldr.outcome: The method cannot authenticate a state change and must never be used for one, but it can hold a session in the Up state at almost no cost. The RFC is Experimental and rates the underlying generator as tolerable for this use only.

today: RFC 9986 is an Experimental RFC and has not been obsoleted or updated. The document classifies itself as outside the IETF Standards Track and says implementations should not be considered compliant with BFD or interoperable with other implementations of this document.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
BFD defines a number of authentication mechanisms, including Simple Password and various other methods based on MD5 and SHA-1 hashes. The benefit of using cryptographic hashes is that they are secure. The downside is that they are expensive and time-consuming on resource-constrained hardware.

When BFD packets are unauthenticated, it is possible for an attacker to forge, modify and replay packets on a link. These attacks have a number of side effects: they can cause parties to believe that a link is down, or that the link is up when it is in fact down.

RFC 9985 defines procedures that enable better scaling of authentication for BFD by splitting the authentication work between more computationally intensive authentication used for significant changes, and less computationally intensive authentication for packets validating that the session is in the Up state.

This document provides the definition of BFD Optimized Authentication Modes using the existing MD5 and SHA-1 authentication mechanisms for the more computationally intensive work. It also defines methods for using the ISAAC mechanism for the less computationally intensive mechanism. ISAAC requires only a few CPU operations per generated 32-bit number, can take a large secret key as a seed, and has an extremely long cycle length. These properties make it ideal for use in BFD. The ISAAC+ document records some cryptanalysis of the mechanism, which addressed an issue with initial seeding, and the method proposed here incorporates recommendations to address that attack.

This document describes an experimental extension to BFD, intended to provide additional insights into what happens when the authentication method defined here is used. It is classified as Experimental and is not part of the IETF Standards Track, and implementations based on it should not be considered compliant with BFD and should not assume interoperability with other implementations that conform to it.
sections.plainLanguage: BFD checks that a link is alive by sending packets very often. Signing every one of them with a cryptographic hash costs more CPU than some small routers can spare. This RFC gives a cheaper proof that the packets really came from the other end: both ends run the same random number generator, and each packet carries the number that generator would produce for it.

sections.title: What Meticulous Keying Means
sections.content:
RFC 5880 uses the terms meticulous keyed and meticulous keying without defining them. Their meaning is found by examining the definition of the sequence number in that document: the sequence number for this packet. For Keyed MD5 Authentication, this value is incremented occasionally. For Meticulous Keyed MD5 Authentication, this value is incremented for each successive packet transmitted for a session, which provides protection against replay attacks.

In this context, meticulous means that the sequence number is incremented on every new packet that is sent, and keyed means that the packets are authenticated through the use of a secret key or keys known to both sender and receiver. The term meticulous keyed therefore refers to the BFD authentication type where each subsequently transmitted packet has a sequence number that is one greater than the immediately previous one and can be authenticated.
sections.plainLanguage: Meticulous means every single packet carries a number that is one higher than the last, so a captured packet can never be replayed later. Keyed means both ends share a secret that the other does not know.

sections.title: Why ISAAC
sections.content:
The mechanism specifies two Optimized BFD Authentication Modes. For the more computationally intensive mechanisms, the existing MD5 and SHA-1 mechanisms are leveraged with small PDU changes necessary to carry the Optimization Mode encoding. For the less computationally intensive mode, the document defines the Meticulous Keyed ISAAC mechanism.

ISAAC is used as a way to generate an infinite stream of pseudorandom numbers, called Auth Keys. With Meticulous Keyed ISAAC, these Auth Keys are used as a signal that the sending party is authentic: only the sending party can generate the correct Auth Keys, so if the receiving party sees a correct Auth Key in a BFD Control Packet in the Up state, then only the sending party could have generated it.

There are many cryptographically secure pseudorandom number generators available, and the document explains why ISAAC was chosen. The goal was a signal that the session was in the Up state in the form of a 32-bit number that is difficult for an attacker to guess, generated from a generator seeded with both public and private data. Because BFD can have packet loss, the generator should also be seekable, so that the BFD state machine can query it, within a small window, for new numbers.

That last property rules out most such generators, as they are not seekable by design: they maintain minimal state, every call modifies the internal state irreversibly, and then produces a new number. It could be possible to use such a generator and manually save many results in a buffer, but ISAAC produces large sets of numbers by design, making it an integrated solution. Most generators are also designed to have small seeds, so any secret key defined by an administrator would have to be hashed before being used as the seed. ISAAC can accept keys up to 8192 octets in length, which is more than sufficient for BFD.

Two instances of ISAAC are created, one for transmission and one for reception, because the inputs for seeding require the locally generated Seed value and the current Your Discriminator value, which are distinct on each side of the session.

The operational sequence is as follows. The administrator provides a secret key used to authenticate each party. When the session transitions into the Up state, the secret key is combined with per-session data to seed ISAAC. The ISAAC process produces a page of 256 32-bit random numbers. The BFD state machine records a sequence number associated with the first entry of that page, and the combination of 256 entries and the sequence number allows the state machine to seek within a 256-packet window at zero cost, through simple addition or subtraction of sequence numbers. If there is a lost packet, the state machine seeks to the entry associated with the received packet and checks whether it contains the expected number. BFD supports packet rates of hundreds of packets per second, and even at those rates 256 entries per page provide for about a second of operation before the next page has to be calculated. As the next page calculation is complex and there is a long period available before the next page is needed, it can be done in the background.

The only downside is that the method does not provide per-packet integrity checks. That limitation is addressed by mandating that Meticulous Keyed ISAAC is only used to signal that the session remains in the Up state. The ISAAC numbers signal that the originator of the packet is authentic, and the state machine verifies that the rest of the packet is well formed and matches the expected state.
sections.plainLanguage: Most random number generators cannot be asked for an old value again, but BFD sometimes needs to, because a packet may have been lost. ISAAC produces its numbers in blocks of 256, so the receiver can find the right one by simple arithmetic. It also accepts long secret keys directly, without hashing them first, and it is cheap enough to run on every packet.

sections.title: The ISAAC Authentication Section
sections.content:
If the Authentication Present bit is set in the header, and the Authentication Type field contains either Optimized MD5 Meticulous Keyed ISAAC Authentication (7) or Optimized SHA-1 Meticulous Keyed ISAAC Authentication (8), and the Optimized Authentication Mode field contains 2, the Authentication Section has the ISAAC format. It carries an Auth Type, an Auth Len of 16 bytes, an Auth Key ID, an Optimized Authentication Mode of 2, a Sequence Number, a 32-bit Seed and a 32-bit Auth Key.

The Auth Type MUST provide for meticulous keying, that is, each packet is authenticated and the Sequence Number field is incremented by one for every packet sent. The Auth Key ID identifies the authentication key in use for this packet, which allows multiple secret keys to be active simultaneously.

The Seed is a 32-bit value used in conjunction with the shared key to configure and initialize the ISAAC pseudorandom number generator. It identifies and secures different streams of random numbers that are generated by ISAAC. The Auth Key carries the 32-bit ISAAC output associated with the sequence number. It is important to note that the Auth Key does not include any summary or hash of the BFD Control Packet: the packet itself is completely unauthenticated.

When the receiving party gets a BFD packet with an expected sequence number and the correct corresponding ISAAC output in the Auth Key field, it knows that only the authentic sending party could have sent that message, and the sending party is therefore Up.

The other two formats keep the same header but carry a digest instead. The MD5 format, used with Auth Type 7 and Optimized Authentication Mode 1, has an Auth Len of 24 bytes and carries the 16-byte MD5 digest for the packet. The SHA-1 format, used with Auth Type 8 and Optimized Authentication Mode 1, has an Auth Len of 28 bytes and carries the 16-byte SHA-1 hash for the packet. Both use the same procedure as the corresponding RFC 5880 authentication modes.
sections.plainLanguage: The packet carries a key identifier, a sequence number, a 32-bit seed and a 32-bit number from the generator. The receiver looks up its own generator output for that sequence number and compares. What is not there is any hash of the packet itself, which is why this format must not be used to signal a state change.

sections.title: Seeding, Sending and Receiving
sections.content:
The receiving system accepts the packet if the key ID matches one of the configured keys, and the Auth Key derived from the selected key, seed and sequence number matches the Auth Key carried in the packet, and the sequence number is strictly greater than the last sequence number received, modulo wrap at 2^32. If any of these criteria do not match, the packet fails validation and is discarded.

On transmission, the Auth Type field MUST be set to one of the two values, the Auth Len MUST be 16, the Auth Key ID MUST be the ID of the current authentication key, the Sequence Number MUST be bfd.XmitAuthSeq, the Seed field MUST carry the current seed for the session, and the Auth Key MUST be the output of ISAAC for the secret key, current seed and sequence number. The Optimized Authentication Mode MUST be 2. The transmit sequence number MUST be incremented by one on each packet in a circular fashion and MUST NOT be incremented by more than one per packet.

On receipt, a packet with no Authentication Section, or with the wrong Auth Type, MUST be discarded, as must one whose Auth Key ID does not match a configured key, whose Optimized Authentication Mode is not 2, or whose Auth Len is not 16. If the sequence number lies outside the range of bfd.RcvAuthSeq plus one up to bfd.RcvAuthSeq plus three times the Detect Multi, the packet MUST be discarded. If the receiver already knows the key and the Seed field does not match the current seed, the packet MUST be discarded.

Calculating the expected ISAAC output can sometimes create a new page of 256 numbers, which is irreversible and destroys the current page. The receiver MUST therefore save a copy of the entire ISAAC state before such a calculation. If the outputs match, the saved copy can be discarded; if they do not, the saved copy MUST be restored.

The Seed is used to identify and secure different streams of random numbers, and each session uses a different Seed, used along with the Your Discriminator field and the secret key to initialize ISAAC. The Seed value MUST be derived from a cryptographically secure random number source. A new Seed value MUST be created every time a session transitions into the Up state, and once the session is Up the Seed MUST NOT change until another state transition occurs. The ISAAC generator is initialized by setting all internal variables to zero and then seeding it with a structure of Seed, Your Discriminator, the secret key and a Counter, which the document uses to avoid the seeding issues described in ISAAC+. Because the size of the seeding buffer is limited, the length of the secret key MUST be no more than 1015 octets. The buffer is filled with repeated copies of the structure, with the Counter incremented from zero for each complete copy. The data is then processed through the randinit function of ISAAC, and numbers are produced 32 bits at a time by calling the isaac function.

The document gives test inputs: Seed 0x0bfd5eed, Your Discriminator 0x4002d15c, the secret key RFC5880June and a counter running from 0 to 50, with the expected Auth Key for sequence number 0 being 9af65d83, for 1 being 44355d56, for 2 being 9334074e, for 3 being b643ef59, for 4 being 74d659f1, for 5 being 8966dc56, for 6 being a1f6f9bc and for 7 being 21895a46.

This construct provides 64 bits of entropy, of which 32 bits are controlled by each party. Each implementation SHOULD randomize its discriminator fields at the start of a session.
sections.plainLanguage: Both ends derive the same stream of numbers from the shared key, the seed and the session's own random values. The receiver works out which number the packet should carry, compares it, and drops the packet if it does not match. The seed is fixed for the lifetime of the session and is never changed while the session is up.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
All security considerations of RFC 5880 and RFC 9985 apply. The distribution of secret keys is typically accomplished using provisioning, and secure distribution for any particular provisioning mechanism is out of scope. Keys generated and distributed out of band are generally limited in the security they can provide, so it is essential that they are selected well and protected when stored.

The security of this proposal depends on the security of the ISAAC algorithm, which has had minimal analysis. While it is believed to be secure enough for this use case, no proof is offered. ISAAC was chosen for the reasons given earlier, as no other option was found suitable: many systems that would implement this have no hardware assistance for cryptographic operations, so any generator based on a block cipher would be unsuitably slow, while where hardware assistance for block ciphers is available ISAAC offers no advantage. As CPUs get faster, more secure methods become better options, such as AES in Output Feedback Mode, ChaCha in software, or other well-understood techniques. For these reasons the ISAAC generator is, at best, tolerable for use in this specification and is completely unsuitable for use in any other IETF protocol.

The security depends strongly on the length of the secret key and on its entropy, and it is RECOMMENDED that the key be 16 octets in length or more. The dependency is mitigated by using two 32-bit numbers, the Your Discriminator field and the ISAAC Seed, both of which are procedurally required to be random; together they serve as a nonce that inhibits offline brute-force dictionary attacks.

On spoofing, Meticulous Keyed ISAAC protects the session against the spoofing of BFD Up packets. If the mechanism is subverted, the periodic more computationally intensive reauthentication limits the time the session is kept inappropriately in the Up state. Packets that are malformed are discarded, as are packets that fail the BFD state machine checks and packets that do not have the correct sequence number, seed and Auth Key. Performing an attack would require the attacker to be on-path and able to perform an active attack, to have the contents of one or more packets, and to have deduced the secret key and be able to correlate the sequence number to the current ISAAC state.

On the reuse of keys, the cryptographic strength of the two mechanisms is significantly different, and it is not settled whether the same key should be used for both. ISAAC is seeded not only with the secret key but also with 32 bits of random data and a sequence number, which increases the difficulty of breaking the key. If different keys are used, they could be misconfigured differently on each side of a link, and a session would immediately drop when it switched to the cheaper mode; suggesting identical keys removes that possibility. But if the ISAAC key is recovered and the same key is used for the MD5 and SHA-1 types, authentication for those mechanisms would be compromised. Implementations are therefore free to use the same key or different keys, and the operator must weigh the security and operational requirements.

On random numbers, the mechanism creates an instance of ISAAC for each session, seeded by the session's secret key and two locally generated random numbers, the Local Discriminator echoed back as Your Discriminator, and a locally generated Seed. These numbers are infrequently generated compared with the use of ISAAC for Auth Keys, so stronger generators with better entropy guarantees can be used, and it is RECOMMENDED that they use a non-ISAAC generator. Random numbers in BFD MUST come from a different source than the ISAAC generator used to create the per-session Auth Keys, and that other instance MUST be distinct and MUST NOT be keyed from any session's secret key.

The YANG module is designed to be accessed through YANG-based management protocols such as NETCONF and RESTCONF, which have to use a secure transport layer and mutual authentication, and the Network Configuration Access Control Model provides the means to restrict access for particular users.
sections.plainLanguage: The honest summary is that the underlying generator has been barely studied, so this is a compromise: cheap enough to run on every packet, but not strong enough for anything else. The protection comes mostly from the secret key and from the two random values that are mixed into it, so the key has to be long and well protected, and the two ends should not reuse it for other purposes.

fields.name: Auth Type
fields.desc: 7 for Optimized MD5 Meticulous Keyed ISAAC, 8 for Optimized SHA-1 Meticulous Keyed ISAAC.

fields.name: Auth Len
fields.desc: Length of the Authentication Section in bytes.

fields.name: Auth Key ID
fields.desc: Which of several configured secret keys is in use.

fields.name: Opt. Mode
fields.desc: 2 for the less computationally intensive authentication type.

fields.name: Sequence Number
fields.desc: Incremented by one for every packet sent, which protects against replay.

fields.name: Seed
fields.desc: A 32-bit seed used with the shared key to initialize the generator and to identify this stream of numbers.

fields.name: Auth Key
fields.desc: The 32-bit ISAAC output for this sequence number. It carries no hash of the packet itself.

viz.caption: HOW A PACKET IS CHECKED WITH THE ISAAC FORMAT

messages.label: BFD PACKET
messages.note: Carries the key ID, the sequence number, the seed and the Auth Key.

messages.label: LOOK UP OUTPUT
messages.note: The receiver computes the number its own generator gives for that sequence number.

messages.label: ACCEPT OR DROP
messages.note: If the numbers match and the sequence number is newer, the session stays Up. Otherwise the packet is discarded.

items.title: Seekable
items.text: Numbers are produced in pages of 256, so the receiver can find the right one for a lost packet by arithmetic.

items.title: Cheap
items.text: Only a few CPU operations per 32-bit number, with the expensive mixing done once per 256 packets.

items.title: Long keys
items.text: Accepts secret keys up to 8192 octets, so an administrator's key can be used directly.

items.title: Long cycle
items.text: A cycle length of 2^8287, far more than the 2^32 sequence numbers a session can use.
